item.title: The path from brain to words is rerouted in opioid addiction
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
Whether spontaneous speech preserves how the brain encoded an experience is unknown. We tested this question in opioid use disorder (OUD), in which drug cues outweigh other rewards. Eighty-two people with OUD and 34 controls watched the opening of the film Trainspotting during functional magnetic resonance imaging, then retold it in their own words. Language-model analyses showed that people with OUD dwelt on craving, personal identification and recovery, devoting more of their retelling to drug scenes. In 65 participants with imaging, this speech bias tracked how strongly the brain had distinguished drug from non-drug scenes during viewing, in left frontoparietal cortex in controls but left temporal cortex in OUD. Direct comparison showed left accumbens coupling positive in OUD and negative in controls, and left superior frontal coupling weaker in OUD. Spontaneous speech thus carries a trace of neural encoding whose route depends on what the experience meant to the speaker.

item.title: Hidden Neural Variability and the Unexplained Cochlear Implant Outcome
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Cochlear implants work, but not equally. After decades of cohort studies, the familiar predictors of outcome (age, duration of deafness, residual hearing, etiology) still leave most of the spread between patients unexplained. Research on how the brain handles degraded speech, audiovisual cues and everyday sounds shows that implant outcome measures test the brain at least as much as the ear. Yet candidacy assessment still examines the cochlea, the auditory nerve and inner-ear anatomy, and rarely the cognitive and structural state of the brain that must learn to use the device. This article argues that undetected neural variability, including cognitive decline, hearing-related atrophy and incidental pathology in brains assumed to be normal, is a plausible and largely unmeasured contributor to the missing variance. It proposes routine cognitive and volumetric phenotyping of implant candidates, and of the control groups against which they are judged. Because the brain restores much of the degraded implant signal through its predictive mechanisms, the article also calls for a new line of work: the development of dedicated tests of predictive brain capacity, a measure currently absent from both candidacy assessment and outcome research.

item.title: Visual-linguistic cues in manual communication: Neural and behavioral responses to Mouthings in sign-naïve perception.
item.description:
Brain and language
Gesture serves as a foundational modality for conveying event structure, providing critical visual information about transitivity and participant roles. Sign languages integrate manual (hand-based) and non-manual (face, torso, head) articulations to encode complex linguistic information. Among these, mouth movements provide phonological and lexical cues, but their role in sign-naïve individuals remains underexplored. This study investigates how sign-naïve individuals process non-manual markers (mouthings) in unfamiliar signed verbs, to explore how linguistic information is extracted from visual stimuli sharing properties with both gesture and sign language. Using EEG, we examined whether lip-reading functions as a linguistic cue or a general perceptual enhancement in non-signers viewing Austrian Sign Language (ÖGS) and non-ÖGS stimuli. Findings reveal distinct neural signatures for manual signs presented with and without congruent mouthings. An early posterior negativity followed by a late posterior positivity suggests that mouthings facilitate lexical access by providing phonological cues that activate stored lexical representations. Conversely, stimuli without mouthings elicited increased anterior activity, reflecting heightened cognitive control demands. Further, telic verbs, which inherently encode event endpoints, showed earlier and stronger facilitation from congruent mouthings compared to atelic verbs. These findings align with the Event Visibility Hypothesis and reinforce the role of visual cues in linguistic comprehension.

item.title: Large language models poorly capture how word order shapes representations of sentence meaning in the human brain.
item.description:
eLife
Large language models based on the transformer architecture are now capable of producing human-like language. But do they encode and process linguistic meaning in a human-like way? Here, we address this question by analysing 7T fMRI data from 30 participants reading 108 sentences each. These sentences are carefully designed to disentangle sentence structure from word meaning, thereby testing whether transformer representations of sentence meaning resemble those formed by the brain. Using representational similarity analysis, we compared representations from eight transformers and eleven other semantic models to brain activity in language regions of interest. We found that while transformer models match brain representations better than models that completely ignore word order, all transformers poorly match human brain representations of sentences that require sensitivity to structural relations such as semantic roles (who did what to whom). Further, transformers were significantly inferior to models explicitly designed to encode the structural relations between words. Our results provide insight into the nature of sentence representation in the brain, highlighting the critical role of sentence structure. They also cast doubt on the claim that transformers represent sentence meaning similarly to the human brain.

item.title: The Concise Language Paradigm in left and right hemisphere stroke: a longitudinal source-localized EEG study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
The mechanisms underlying language recovery after stroke remain poorly understood. Most previous studies have either focused on language comprehension or production and/or relied on hemodynamic measures, with limited complementary electrophysiological evidence. Here, we combined the Concise Language Paradigm (CLaP), assessing comprehension and production, with individualized electroencephalography (EEG) source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke language function and changes in hemispheric dominance over time. In two sessions, we tested stroke-free controls, individuals with left hemisphere (LH) or right hemisphere (RH) stroke. Participants with stroke were assessed two and seven months post-stroke. EEG data were analyzed using event-related potentials and time-frequency representations, followed by source reconstruction based on state-of-the-art individual MRI-derived forward models. Laterality indices were calculated to assess changes in hemispheric dominance between sessions. Behaviorally, the LH group showed low performance at two months followed by overall improvement, whereas the RH group mainly improved in functional communication. EEG activity was significantly modulated by task condition across comprehension and production contrasts. Source-level results in controls were consistent with established language-related networks, serving as regions of interest for the stroke analyses. In the stroke groups, hemispheric dominance differed between LH and RH stroke participants, with LH participants showing systematic shifts from left- to right-hemisphere dominance between sessions, if not already right-hemisphere dominant at two months. Our study provides evidence on comprehension and production performance after stroke using a single paradigm. These findings demonstrate dynamic changes in hemispheric dominance during post-stroke recovery, ultimately highlighting the value of individualized EEG source reconstruction to investigate post-stroke plasticity.

item.title: Unstable word form representations and greater reliance on right hemisphere during word learning in adults with a history of developmental language disorder
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Impairment in acquiring new vocabulary is a persistent deficit in developmental language disorder (DLD), but its cortical substrates remain unclear. We investigated learning of new words in young adults with DLD and typically developing (TD) control participants using magnetoencephalography (MEG). Participants were exposed to spoken real words and two sets of pseudowords, with shared beginnings, in two MEG sessions. One set of pseudowords was actively trained for three days, paired with fantasy animal pictures. Both groups learned new pseudowords, but adults with DLD recalled fewer items and confused similar sounding pseudowords more often than TD adults. MEG recordings revealed robust left temporal learning effects in both groups, along with left inferior frontal involvement. The DLD group additionally showed stronger right-hemispheric involvement and a significant right temporal learning effect for the newly learned words. Furthermore, only the DLD group showed changes in the left and right temporal responses for the real words after the learning phase, indicating altered lexical access for familiar words after integration of new word forms with overlapping phonology into the mental lexicon. Together, the findings suggest persisting problems in creating and accessing stable and distinctive phonological memory representations for word forms in adults with DLD, along with altered hemispheric balance in processing.

item.title: The joint modulation of language distance and task demands on the neural mechanisms underlying bilingual lexical processing
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Whether bilinguals share the same neural mechanisms for processing their first language (L1) and second language (L2) is a question of broad interest to researchers. Existing studies have accumulated substantial evidence, yet findings remain divergent. The primary sources of inconsistency lie in the language distance between bilinguals' L1 and L2, as well as differences in experimental tasks. Leveraging the advantages of meta-analysis, the present study examined brain activation patterns during L1 and L2 lexical processing in two groups of bilinguals: Chinese–English bilinguals with distant language distance (logographically–alphabetic) and alphabetic–alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance—across different tasks (phonological and semantic). Results showed that in phonological tasks, Chinese–English bilinguals recruited the left inferior parietal lobule/supramarginal gyrus more for L2, a region implicated in orthography-to-phonology conversion; in contrast, alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance shared overlapping neural mechanisms for L1 and L2. In semantic tasks, Chinese–English bilinguals engaged the left middle frontal gyrus and left precuneus more for L1 to support orthography-to-semantics conversion. In contrast, alphabetic bilinguals recruited the left middle temporal gyrus more for L1 for phonology-to-semantics conversion, and engaged language-control regions including the left middle frontal gyrus/inferior frontal gyrus, insula, and inferior parietal lobule more for L2. Further comparisons of brain activation during language-switching tasks between the two bilingual groups also revealed that alphabetic bilinguals with close language distance required greater involvement of executive control regions. Collectively, these findings indicate that the differential brain activation patterns observed when bilinguals process L1 and L2 arise from differences in underlying cognitive processes, jointly driven by language distance and task demands.

item.title: The uncinate fasciculus in frontotemporal dementia subtypes: A systematic review and meta-analysis of diffusion-tensor imaging studies.
item.description:
Journal of Alzheimer's disease : JAD
BackgroundFrontotemporal dementia (FTD) is a leading cause of early-onset neurodegeneration with selective frontal and temporal lobe degeneration. Despite well-characterized gray and white matter atrophy patterns across FTD subtypes, the extent of degeneration of the uncinate fasciculus (UF) tract has not been systematically quantified across FTD subtypes.ObjectiveTo compare uncinate fasciculus fractional anisotropy, mean diffusivity, radial diffusivity, and axial diffusivity between frontotemporal dementia subtypes and healthy controls.MethodsWe systematically searched PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science and performed a random-effects meta-analysis of diffusion tensor imaging studies published between 2011 and October 2025 according to PRISMA 2020 guidelines.ResultsWe systematically reviewed 11 studies and performed a meta-analysis of 540 participants across 10 studies. We found that all FTD subtypes demonstrated significant degeneration of the UF compared to controls. The greatest effect sizes were observed when comparing the left UF between the semantic variant primary progressive aphasia (svPPA) and controls (FA: SMD = -2.5396, 95% CI: -3.7914, -1.2878, p < 0.0001; RD: SMD = 2.2414, 95% CI:1.7972, 2.6855, p < 0.0001; AD: SMD = 1.9831, 95% CI: 1.1434, 2.8227, p < 0.0001; MD: SMD = 2.5268, 95% CI: 1.9993, 3.0542, p < 0.0001), while the behavioral variant (bvFTD) showed the largest reduction in right UF fractional anisotropy. Within-group analyses revealed significant left-right asymmetry in svPPA and non-fluent aphasia (nfvPPA), with greater left UF involvement, while bvFTD and controls showed no hemispheric differences.ConclusionsWe highlight the UF as a promising tract for understanding disease mechanisms and developing imaging biomarkers in FTD.

item.title: Individual Differences in Sustained Attention Tune Semantic Abstraction in Neural Encoding of Narratives
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Neural encoding modeling for narrative comprehension -- using LLM embeddings to predict the temporal dynamics of neural activation -- is widely used to evaluate how well the brain represents certain semantic information. This approach, however, typically collapses semantic representation into a scalar fidelity score aggregated across participants, overlooking potentially rich individual differences and qualitative differences in naturalistic neural representations. In the current study, we addressed this gap by investigating how neural semantic encoding varies across individuals with sustained attention, and whether this difference is qualitative in addition to quantitative. Using fMRI data from 49 participants listening to an audiobook, Le Petit Prince, in English, we trained encoding models with GPT-2 embeddings at varying layers and forecasting lengths. Encoding models trained on high-level embeddings (from the 8th layer of GPT-2) showed significant brain-LLM alignment in 73 of 122 cortical and subcortical ROIs, concentrated in the temporal cortex and the default mode network. Functional connectivity strength in a validated connectome-based predictive model of sustained attention correlated with encoding performance in 18 ROIs, most strongly in the insula and in control and attention networks, with no ROI showing significant opposite relationship. Decomposing semantic information by levels of abstraction showed that the neural signature of sustained attention was selectively associated with a greater proportion of high-level gist information encoded in the frontoparietal and attention networks, while the opposite relationship emerged for proportion of low-level information. Sustained attention scores further predicted stronger predictive coding of upcoming narrative content across multiple networks across the whole brain (control, default mode, salience/ventral attention, limbic, and somatomotor networks). These findings suggest that sustained attention does not uniformly amplify neural semantic encoding, but instead shifts neural representations toward more compressed, gist-level formats that support anticipation of upcoming content. Individual differences in brain-LLM alignment can be a signature of representational strategy rather than noise, with potential utility for cognitive phenotyping.

item.title: Neural correlates of infant dialect discrimination: An fNIRS study.
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
The present study investigated the neural correlates of infant discrimination of very similar linguistic varieties (Quebecois and Parisian French) using functional Near InfraRed Spectroscopy. In line with previous behavioral and electrophysiological data, there was no evidence that 3-month-olds discriminated the two regional accents, whereas 5-month-olds did, with the locus of discrimination in left anterior perisylvian regions. These neuroimaging results suggest that a developing language network relying crucially on left perisylvian cortices sustains infants’ discrimination of similar linguistic varieties within this early period of infancy.

item.title: Neuropharmacology of language: ERP evidence for catecholaminergic modulation of syntactic processing.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
A few studies have shown that brain catecholamines are implicated in language comprehension. However, the specific cognitive processes they modulate remain underexplored. We hypothesized that catecholamines enhance the unification of syntactic roles and word meanings into coherent multiword structures. This study combined electroencephalography and psychopharmacology to examine the effects of a catecholaminergic stimulant (methylphenidate) on processing sentences containing local syntactic ambiguities. Methylphenidate amplified the P600 event-related potential effect, which has been linked to the recruitment of cognitive resources for processing sentences with increased syntactic load. The drug's impact on semantic processing was subtler, showing a suggestive attenuation of the N400 effect to ambiguous sentences. Furthermore, the increase in the P600 effect under methylphenidate was most pronounced in participants with lower working memory capacity. This study provides evidence for linking catecholamine activity to syntactic unification in healthy individuals. Elevated catecholamine levels appear to increase the cognitive effort invested in syntactic unification, and to support the dynamic prioritization of syntactic information when contextual demands require it.

item.title: Adult aphasic status epilepticus: A systematic review and patient-level synthesis of clinical phenotypes and multimodal diagnostic evidence.
item.description:
Epilepsy & behavior : E&B
Background Aphasic status epilepticus (ASE) is an uncommon manifestation of focal status epilepticus in which aphasia is the sole or predominant clinical feature. Recognition may be difficult because consciousness can be relatively preserved, convulsive activity may be absent, and the presentation can mimic acute stroke. Objective To characterize diagnostic phenotypes of adult ASE and synthesize clinical, electrographic, and neuroimaging features across published cases. Methods We conducted a systematic review and patient-level synthesis of adult ASE cases. Eligible patients were adjudicated as definite or probable ASE using prespecified criteria. Clinical phenotype, electroencephalographic (EEG) findings, neuroimaging, initial diagnostic impressions, treatment, and language outcomes were extracted. Results Ninety-nine publications contributed 168 adults with ASE, including 89 definite and 79 probable cases. Aphasia was the sole manifestation in 42.9% and predominant in 57.1%, while consciousness was preserved in 78.0%. Ictal EEG activity or electrographic status epilepticus was documented in 53.0%, and 41.7% had supportive epileptiform abnormalities. Among cases with interpretable EEG laterality, 92.7% were left-lateralized. Peri-ictal MRI abnormalities occurred in 41.2% of performed interpretable studies. Among 55 patients with interpretable functional perfusion or metabolic imaging, hyperperfusion was reported in 32. FDG-PET hypermetabolism was treated as a distinct metabolic finding. Stroke or transient ischemic attack was the most frequent reported initial impression (44.2%). Complete language recovery was reported in 77.4% of evaluable patients. Conclusions Published adult ASE cases show a heterogeneous phenotype in which recognition commonly rests on concordance between language disturbance and focal EEG abnormalities, with peri-ictal imaging providing complementary evidence. These findings do not establish diagnostic accuracy of individual features or multimodal combinations.

item.title: Altered Cortico-cerebellar effective connectivity of the Visuo-attentional system is associated with READ1 deletion in developmental dyslexia.
item.description:
NeuroImage. Clinical
Developmental dyslexia (DD) is a heritable neurodevelopmental disorder associated with altered brain connectivity. The influence of genetic risks on cortico-cerebellar effective connectivity (EC) remains unclear. The present study investigates how reading proficiency and the READ1 deletion (READ1d) in the DCDC2 gene modulate visuo-attentional network dynamics. Functional MRI data were acquired in 78 children (DD and typical readers, with/without READ1d) performing a coherent motion detection task. EC within a seven-region visuo-attentional network, including magnocellular, ventral attention, and cerebellar (crus I) regions, was estimated using Dynamic Causal Modelling. Group-level effects were assessed using Parametric Empirical Bayes within a hierarchical Bayesian framework, testing reading proficiency, READ1d status, and their interaction (posterior probability threshold, Pp > 0.95). Reading proficiency was associated with increased cerebellar influence on visual and frontal regions, alongside reduced intra-cortical connectivity within dorsal stream pathways. The presence of READ1d was associated with reduced EC from primary visual and cerebellar regions to magnocellular and ventral attention networks, and increased intra-cortical interactions. The interaction between DD and READ1d revealed further reductions in cortico-cerebellar connectivity and altered network dynamics. Group-level analyses revealed EC differences in cortico-cerebellar pathways, which are reported as exploratory findings. Cortico-cerebellar EC is modulated by both reading proficiency and genetic susceptibility. Altered cerebellar contributions to visuo-attentional processes may represent a potential imaging-genetic signature of dyslexia, warranting replication in independent samples and validation through longitudinal and multimodal approaches.

item.title: The Influence of Contralesional Brain Age Gradients on Chronic Stroke Aphasia Severity and Treatment Response.
item.description:
The Journal of neuroscience : the official journal of the Society for Neuroscience
The adult brain follows normative aging trajectories, yet stroke abruptly disrupts this process. Beyond the focal lesion, undamaged regions can deviate from expected aging due to diaschisis or pre-existing vulnerabilities, reflecting tissue health that may constrain recovery. Chronic post-stroke aphasia, a persistent language disorder, shows wide individual variability in severity and treatment response, and these differences are not fully captured by lesion characteristics or demographic factors. Further, prior imaging biomarkers have been difficult to scale because they rely on specialized acquisitions or nonstandardized analytical pipelines. Here, we used a standardized, lifespan-informed brain age model (volBrain) trained on large public datasets to quantify regional deviations from normative aging using only routine structural MRI (T1-weighted). In 188 individuals with chronic stroke (67 female, 121 male), regional aging deviations in the contralesional hemisphere explained aphasia severity beyond lesion volume, lesion location, and basic demographics. In a treated subgroup, baseline brain aging patterns also predicted language gains that persisted 6 months after therapy, indicating prognostic value. By characterizing how individual brains diverge from expected aging, this approach captures variation in tissue integrity that is relevant for both impairment and recovery. This provides a scalable framework that can be integrated across sites and studies, linking normative aging models with post-stroke prognostics and informing precision neurorehabilitation.

item.title: Neurophysiological dynamics related to perception, action, and language in schizophrenia.
item.description:
Science advances
Schizophrenia disrupts both how people perceive the world and how they express and act on their thoughts, yet these symptoms are usually studied separately. Using magnetoencephalography during multisensory and motor tasks, we tested whether reduced event-related beta-band (15 to 30 hertz) modulation, a signal implicated in predictive control, provides a candidate neural marker across these domains. Compared to healthy individuals, patients showed diminished beta changes during sensory processing and movement completion, suggesting reduced flexibility in updating internal models. This neural pattern covaried with audiovisual simultaneity-judgment behavior, disorganized natural speech, and greater clinical severity. These findings suggest that distributed beta modulation may serve as a candidate cross-domain marker associated with perceptual, motor, and language disturbances in schizophrenia, motivating future studies that directly test predictive updating mechanisms.

item.title: Towards semantic brain-computer interfacing: The graded inventory of semantic triggers (GIST) paradigm.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Objective Semantic Brain-Computer Interfaces (sBCIs) aim to decode conceptual information directly from neural activity, enabling more efficient and natural communication for individuals with severe motor impairments. However, existing approaches are often confounded by stimulus-driven perceptual processes and lack a reliable means of tagging the moment of concept formation. We introduce the Graded Inventory of Semantic Triggers (GIST), a novel electroencephalography (EEG) paradigm designed to elicit semantic retrieval from graded verbal clues with precise temporal alignment. Approach: EEG data were recorded from 14 participants performing the GIST task across three semantic categories (food, musical instruments, and body parts). Target neural activity was aligned to each participant's self-reported moment of semantic retrieval (spacebar press), enabling response-locked analysis. Here, we propose a staged framework where the first comprises a Conformer-based encoder trained on pooled data using a hybrid contrastive objective that combines instance-level consistency and cross-participant class alignment with domain-adversarial learning to reduce participant-specific information. In the second stage, the frozen encoder is transferred to a held-out participant whose data played no part in Stage 1, and a support vector machine is calibrated on that participant's own labelled items under a nested leave-one-item-out protocol. Results: Above-chance semantic decoding was achieved in all three pairwise tasks. Mean accuracies were 73.4% (Body vs. Food), 70.7% (Body vs. Music), and 68.2% (Food vs. Music). Participant-level permutation tests were significant in 9/11 participants for Body vs. Food and 8/11 for each of the other tasks (p < 0.05). The pre-response interval at [-1.5s, -0.5s] was the most discriminative. Significance: The GIST paradigm enables controlled elicitation and temporal alignment of semantic processing while reducing perceptual confounds. Combined with cross-participant representation pretraining and participant-specific calibration, the results demonstrate above-chance decoding of semantic categories from EEG in individuals excluded from representation learning, supporting the feasibility of sBCIs.

item.title: Naturalistic spatial education engages distinct neural processes for mental rotation, cognitive load, and linguistic demands.
item.description:
Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences of the United States of America
Neuroscience studies typically isolate spatial cognition using simplified tasks targeting a single cognitive process. However, during formal spatial education, the brain rarely performs one cognitive operation at a time. Here, we used functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) to assess neural systems involved in dynamically processing an educational spatial visualization lesson. We quantified lesson content using an instructional-design framework capturing variation in spatial complexity, cognitive load, and verbal density. We then characterized how instructional demands modulated brain function using content-evoked responses, functional connectivity, and network-centrality. Spatial transformations during instruction robustly recruited parietal and premotor regions, which were linearly modulated by spatial complexity. This parietal dominance aligns with theories that these areas encode geometric and quantitative dimensions. In contrast, domain-general frontal activity tracked overall processing demands, and language regions tracked verbal density. Activity also varied with learners' spatial abilities: higher spatial performers showed stronger modulation of parietal and premotor regions as spatial demands increased, and greater domain-general modulation across content types. Thus, the same circuitry representing spatial transformations during instruction also reflects individual variation in spatial cognition. Parietal regions showed the highest centrality and strongest within-network coherence, marking them as the central hub of the system, and distinguishing them from less central and less coherent domain-general regions. Together, the findings reveal how the brain dynamically decomposes complex spatial instruction, preserving parietal-centered spatial processing, while coordinating support from premotor, domain-general, and language systems. These findings begin to reveal how spatial cognition operates within the complexity of formal instruction.

item.title: A New Web-Based Word-Picture Matching Test Reveals Psycholinguistic Effects on Word-Level Reading and Auditory Comprehension in Aphasia.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Purpose Word reading comprehension deficits, often measured by word-to-picture matching (WtPM) tasks, are common in aphasia and alexia. To specify the nature of comprehension deficits, WtPM tasks should manipulate psycholinguistic features, have matched written and auditory versions, and provide normed scores measuring speed and accuracy. Here we present a novel web-based WtPM task that meets those needs. We use it to assess word comprehension deficits in left-hemisphere stroke survivors (LHSS). Method We examined scores for the novel auditory and written WtPM task in a normative sample (n = 62) and an LHSS sample (n = 63). Mixed-effects models examined accuracy and response time in both groups, and an analysis of variance compared efficiency between the groups. Correlations compared written WtPM performance and item difficulty to auditory WtPM, written lexical decision, and oral reading. A k -means clustering analysis examined deficit patterns in the LHSS group. Results WtPM performance was modulated by modality, frequency, and regularity and was impaired in the LHSS group. Written WtPM performance and item difficulty were correlated with auditory WtPM and written lexical decision in both groups and with oral reading in the LHSS group. Over half of the LHSS sample had frank deficits on at least one WtPM task. Comprehension deficits in individual LHSS were often modulated by input modality, word frequency, and regularity. Conclusions We present a clinically accessible WtPM task that captures individual patterns of word comprehension impairment in both written and auditory modalities. The use of efficiency scores allows for the assessment of mild impairments that are missed by ceiling effects on currently available tasks. Input modality, frequency, and regularity affect word comprehension as measured by WtPM. Individual stroke survivors present with different combinations of these effects, which may help to identify specific deficits and spared abilities that can guide reading comprehension treatment. Supplemental material https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.33968839.

item.title: Altered language network microstructure links with impaired language function and development in very preterm/very low birth weight born adults.
item.description:
NeuroImage
Premature birth is associated with impaired language function. In premature-born children, language function has been linked with microstructural alterations of the language network.Whether these brain-language associations persist into adulthood remains unclear. We investigated the microstructural properties of major dorsal and ventral language pathways in very preterm/very low birth weight (VPT/VLBW) adults and their associations with language performance in adulthood and childhood. Sixty-three VPT/VLBW and eighty full-term-born adults (mean age 26.8 years) underwent diffusion-weighted imaging and language assessment. The arcuate fasciculus, superior longitudinal fasciculus, uncinate fasciculus and inferior fronto-occipital fasciculus were reconstructed using probabilistic tractography from which fractional anisotropy (FA) and mean diffusivity (MD) measures were extracted. Adult language function was assessed via the Regensburg word fluency test, rapid automatized naming and verbal IQ; childhood language was assessed at the mean age of 8 using the Kaufman Assessment Battery for children. We observed altered language network microstructure in VPT/VLBW participants, illustrated by lower FA and higher MD in the SLF and UF. These microstructural alterations were associated with language function in adulthood, but also with language development in childhood. We found that the association between tract microstructure and language abilities differed between groups. Our results demonstrate altered language network microstructure in premature born adults, which links with impaired language function and development. These findings extend previous work by comprehensively characterizing the adult dorsal and ventral language network and relating its microstructural properties to language function across development. The selective follow-up sample may limit generalizability to the broader VPT/VLBW population.

item.title: Mapping the brain signature of dyslexia risk onto histamine, acetylcholine and glutamate receptor systems
item.description:
[预印本] medRxiv
The brain differences of dyslexia are well described and its genetic risk is now measurable; the brain systems that connect the two are unknown. That link decides which measures complement one another in early identification and which systems intervention research should examine. Here we compared large-scale polygenic score maps of brain structure in dyslexia with normative maps of brain neurotransmitter systems. The structural signature of genetic liability aligned with the cortical distribution of neurotransmitter systems. The strongest and most consistent alignment appeared for the histamine H3 receptor, the vesicular acetylcholine transporter (VAChT) and the N-methyl-D-aspartate (NMDA) glutamate receptor. The alignment was most pronounced in cingulate, medial and superior frontal cortex and the paracentral lobule. The H3 alignment held after adjustment for cortical position and for metabolic and cognitive reference maps. Once the component common to all nineteen maps and position were removed together, no individual system remained significant, while the shared component itself aligned with liability. The signature therefore follows the topography these systems share. In 169 children, per-person alignment with the H3 map related to reading skill with the opposite sign to liability. To our knowledge, this is the first study to relate the structural signature of genetic liability for dyslexia to normative maps of neurotransmitter receptor and transporter density. It places that signature within the shared geography of the systems that set attention, arousal and synaptic plasticity during learning, and gives the genetics of dyslexia a testable biological axis.

item.title: Plasticity in Human Brain Language Areas After Stroke: What Can the Right Hemisphere Do?
item.description:
The Neuroscientist : a review journal bringing neurobiology, neurology and psychiatry
Among the most devastating effects stroke can have on the lives of survivors and those around them are language production and comprehension impairments. The most notable of them - often given the joint diagnostic label of "aphasia" despite their heterogeneity and dissociability - are associated with damage to the brain's left hemisphere, which, in large part for this reason, is considered the "language-dominant" hemisphere. However, the right hemisphere's contribution to language should not be underestimated and may in fact be key to understanding the possibilities and limitations of neuroplasticity for supporting language recovery after stroke. Thus, in this review, we focus on the role of the right hemisphere in supporting human language function, in the neurologically healthy brain and after stroke. We discuss the remarkable capability of the right hemisphere to support normal language abilities after a large left-hemisphere stroke early in life, the more limited capacity for right-hemisphere language support after left-hemisphere stroke in adulthood, and potential interactions between typically left-hemisphere dominant "core" language functions with language functions typically thought to be right-hemisphere dominant, such as emotional prosody. We conclude by highlighting gaps in current knowledge and suggesting areas for future research.

item.title: Delineating neural contributions to electroencephalogram-based speech decoding.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Objective . Speech Brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) have emerged as a pivotal technology in facilitating communication for individuals with speech impairments. Utilizing electroencephalography (EEG) for noninvasive speech BCIs offers an accessible and affordable solution, potentially benefiting a broader audience. However, EEG-based speech decoding remains controversial especially for overt speech, due to difficulties in separating speech-related neural activities from myoelectric potential artifacts generated during articulation. Moreover, because paradigms for collecting covert speech data are inherently less scalable than those for overt speech, whether the neural dynamics underlying EEG-based decoding of overt speech are also present during covert speech remains an open and practically important question. Approach . Here we aim to delineate the extent of the neural contributions to EEG-based speech decoding, and the degree to which the underlying neural dynamics are shared across overt and covert speech, by employing Explainable AI techniques to a convolutional neural network predicting spoken words based on signals obtained by ultra-high-density (uhd)-EEG. Main results . We found that electrode-wise contributions to the decoding cannot be explained by their mutual information with electromyography (EMG). Furthermore, contributing periods of speech to EEG-based decoding are distinct from those to decoding solely relying on EMG. In contrast, there are significant overlaps in signal timings contributing to EEG-based decoding, regardless of vocal conditions such as overt or covert speech. Notably, the denoising process successfully enhanced the decoding contribution from electrodes within speech-related brain areas for all speech conditions. Significance

item.title: The spatial extent of fast ripples is associated with cognitive and language deficits in children with focal epilepsy: An exploratory SEEG study.
item.description:
Epilepsy & behavior : E&B
Objective To determine if the spatial extent of interictal fast ripples in focal epilepsy patients is associated with brain dysfunction. Methods Thirty pediatric focal epilepsy patients who underwent SEEG investigation had their cognitive and language deficits assessed in scales of 0 to 4. Fast ripples (250-500 Hz), ripples (80-250 Hz), and IEDs were automatically detected in 10 min during NREM sleep. We fitted linear models to the relationship between the cognitive deficit scale and the spatial spread of the interictal neurophysiologic events (number of channels with rate of events > 10 % of maximum rate). For the language deficit, we computed the Spearman correlation between the median rate of events in all brain regions and the deficit scale. Results Cognitive deficit scale was significantly associated with the number of channels with fast ripples (p = 0.049), not so with ripples (p = 0.31), IEDs (p = 0.31). The potential confound of number of explored channels did not improve the fitting of the models. Language deficits were not correlated with the number of channels showing interictal events. However, from all brain regions the most statistically significant correlations (p < 0.01) were between median fast ripple rates in the left and right pars opercularis and triangularis of the inferior frontal gyrus (Broca's area and its contralateral counterpart) with r = 0.66, p = 0.003 (18 patients), in the superior temporal gyrus in the language dominant hemisphere with r = 0.72, p = 0.005 (13 patients), and the dominant basal temporal region with r = 0.79, p = 0.006 (10 patients). Median rates of IEDs and ripples exhibited lower correlation with language deficits in these regions. Conclusion Widespread fast ripples are associated with increased cognitive deficits, and language deficiencies are correlated with fast ripple rates in brain regions associated with language. The extent of fast-ripple activity was associated with cognitive deficit severity in this cohort, whereas the corresponding associations for ripples and IEDs did not reach statistical significance.

item.title: Combined eye tracking and electroencephalography during referential selection in dyadic interaction.
item.description:
Behavior research methods
Understanding language in real-world interaction requires methods that integrate auditory, visual, and neural signals. We present a proof-of-concept study combining mobile electroencephalography (EEG) and eye tracking to investigate referential selection during dyadic communication. Using a simplified version of the director task, pairs of participants engaged in naturalistic object-movement instructions while EEG and gaze data were recorded and synchronized via LabStreamingLayer, allowing us to calculate overlap-corrected, regression-based event-related potentials (rERPs) time-locked to spoken nouns and to participants' fixations, focusing on the N400/P300 (300-500 ms) and later (500-800 ms) time windows. Our results show that gaze behavior and fixation-related potentials provide crucial information for interpreting language-related ERPs: Targets competing with occluded referents elicited a stronger posterior positivity consistent with greater attentional demands. Fixation timing systematically modulated neural responses. Contrary to predictions, competitors received little visual attention, indicating that participants prioritized task-relevant information. These findings highlight the potential of multimodal data integration for understanding attentional and predictive mechanisms in real-world communication. Importantly, we show that established analytic techniques, such as artifact subspace reconstruction, independent component analysis, and linear deconvolution for ERP calculation, apply to noisy, naturalistic datasets. In addition, we provide a subsampling sensitivity approach to test the stability of the effects across different sample sizes. This study provides a methodological framework linking gaze and neural activity during interactive language processing. All preprocessing and analysis scripts, along with example datasets, are openly available on OSF ( https://osf.io/5ds4z ; a modified and optimized Python implementation is also available on GitHub: https://github.com/XlinCLab/DGAME ).

item.title: Bridging the Gap Between Design and Access: Toward Visual Scene Displays for Brain-Computer Interface Use in Augmentative and Alternative Communication by Children.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Purpose Brain-computer interface (BCI) may support communication and computer interaction through neural signals such as the P300 event-related potential (ERP). As a step toward integrating photographic visual scene displays (VSDs) in BCI, this study examined the feasibility of incorporating contextual, naturalistic scenes in which communication items were embedded asymmetrically. Method To evaluate the effects of contextual scene use, 24 neurotypical children aged 8-13 years completed three experimental conditions: (1) a contextual scene with asymmetrical item placement, (2) an asymmetrical arrangement of the same items without contextual information, and (3) a standard grid. Electroencephalogram data were analyzed for the N170, P300, and N400 ERP components, and offline (predicted) BCI augmentative and alternative communication accuracy was calculated. Results The results showed that asymmetry increased frontal and centro-parietal P300 amplitudes, and the scene enhanced occipital N170. Offline BCI performance was similar across the scene and grid conditions, and participants rated the scene as more visually appealing. Conclusion These findings indicate that asymmetry and contextual embedding within scenes may enhance neural engagement and user experience, providing a preliminary foundation for considering photographic VSDs into pediatric BCI research.

item.title: Sentence Completion Expressive Language Task-Preschool: Preliminary Evidence of Validity and Feasibility for the Neuroimaging Environment.
item.description:
Journal of speech, language, and hearing research : JSLHR
Purpose This preliminary investigation occurred across two studies and examined validity, discriminant accuracy, and feasibility of the Sentence Completion Expressive Language Task-Preschool (SCELT-P) for characterizing language production in a neuroimaging environment for typically developing (TD) preschoolers and those with developmental language disorder (DLD). Method Two separate studies were completed. Study 1 (validity) included 82 preschoolers (50% female; 69 TD, 13 DLD) aged 4;0 (years;months) to 5;11 (M age = 4;7). All children were assessed using standardized language measures (e.g., Clinical Evaluation of Language Fundamentals Preschool-Second Edition), a play-based language sample (analyzed using Developmental Sentence Scoring), and the 30-item SCELT-P (outside the neuroimaging environment), later streamlined to 20 items (SCELT-P Revised [SCELT-PR]). Study 2 (feasibility) included 14 preschoolers (M age = 4;9, 43% female; nine TD, five with DLD) that were assessed using the SCELT-P (inside the neuroimaging environment) and functional magnetic resonance imaging using a sparse acquisition approach with a "listen" (passive) and "listen + speak" (active) condition implemented using DirectRT software. Results In Study 1, the SCELT-P and SCELT-PR demonstrated high reliability, including interrater (intraclass correlation coefficient = .99), test-retest (r = .86 and .80, respectively), and internal consistency (Cronbach's α > .86 and .83, respectively), and similar strong criterion validity (r = . 53-.84). Area under the curve analyses (.91) revealed both versions also evidenced fair sensitivity (.88 and .87) and specificity (.85) rates with a cutoff score of 15.5 and 9.5, respectively. In Study 2, 89% of TD preschoolers and 60% of preschoolers with DLD successfully completed the SCELT-P/R inside the neuroimaging environment, with activation maps illustrating relatively similar neurobiological characteristics across preschoolers in some brain regions. Conclusion The SCELT-P, including its streamlined version, the SCELT-PR, holds promise as a reliable and valid task for including 4- to 5-year-olds in the neuroimaging environment to inform neural and cognitive systems involved in language development. Supplemental material https://doi.org/10.23641/asha.34543209.

item.title: EEG Resting-State Beta Band Dynamic Functional Connectivity Reveals State-Dependent Disruption of Language Network Lateralisation in First-Episode Schizophrenia.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
Language disorganisation is a core feature of schizophrenia with significant functional consequences. However, its neurophysiological substrates remain poorly characterised, particularly in the early stages of the illness. This study investigated whether first-episode schizophrenia (FES) is associated with disruption in the organisation of language-network lateralisation, using both static and dynamic functional connectivity metrics in the EEG beta band. Thirty-one FES patients and 32 age-matched healthy volunteer subjects (HVS) underwent resting-state 64-channel EEG. Source-level connectivity was estimated using the weighted phase lag index with sliding windows, yielding 979 connectivity matrices per participant. Brain network states (BNS) were identified via k-means clustering. Static connectivity was obtained by time-averaging. Temporal features, graph-theoretical metrics, and language-network laterality indices were extracted for both whole-network and language-specific analyses. Group comparisons used permutation-based tests with family-wise error correction. Static connectivity yielded no significant group differences in any metric. Dynamic analysis identified six BNS. FES showed a significant increase in the variability of the temporal dynamics and graph-theory features of BNS5, a state characterised by parieto-occipital dominance. The core language network laterality index was significantly reduced in FES within BNS1, a state characterised by auditory-visual dominance. BNS1 occurrence correlated negatively with language disorganisation scores. Dynamic BNS-specific language network metrics correlated with verbal fluency performance exclusively in FES. These findings demonstrate that language dysfunction in early psychosis is expressed as state-dependent disruption of brain network stability and language lateralisation, detectable only through dynamic connectivity analysis.

item.title: Modeling Paralinguistic Features for Speech Neuroprostheses: A Systematic Review
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Recent advances in brain-computer interface (BCI) technology have brought speech neuroprostheses closer to restoring naturalistic communication for individuals with severe motor or speech impairments. Although current systems can decode phonemic and lexical information from cortical activity, they often fail to capture paralinguistic dimensions such as intonation, prosody, loudness, and affect that are essential for conveying emotion and intent. This review synthesizes emerging research on modeling and incorporating paralinguistic features into speech neuroprosthetic design. Foundational studies have mapped the cortical organization of speech production, identifying articulatory somatotopy within the sensorimotor cortex and functional subdivisions across planning, phonological, and semantic representations. More recent work has characterized expressive encoding within the ventral precentral and supplementary motor areas, while peripheral and multimodal sensing approaches have demonstrated promising accuracy in decoding emotional states. Collectively, these findings signal a shift toward closed-loop neuroprosthetic systems that integrate affective modulation with linguistic decoding, enabling restoration of speech that is not only intelligible but expressively human.

item.title: Functional neural activity and connectivity deficits underlying vocal auditory feedback control in post-stroke aphasia: An fMRI study.
item.description:
Clinical neurophysiology : official journal of the International Federation of Clinical Neurophysiology
Objective This study investigated the functional neural activity and connectivity correlates of disrupted sensorimotor integration underlying vocal production and motor control deficits in post-stroke aphasia. Methods fMRI data were acquired from 15 aphasia and 15 control participants during vocalization of speech vowel sounds under altered auditory feedback with randomized ± 100-cents pitch-shift stimuli. Results We found that stroke-induced brain damage in aphasia was associated with diminished activation within left-hemisphere dorsal stream networks, including premotor and motor cortices, posterior superior temporal regions, and supramarginal gyrus. Functional connectivity analysis revealed reduced left-hemisphere coupling between posterior superior temporal gyrus (pSTG) and dorsal and ventral precentral speech areas (dPSA and vPSA) in aphasia, indicating disrupted auditory-motor integration. Aphasia participants exhibited reduced following and opposing (i.e., compensatory) vocal responses to pitch-shifted auditory feedback, reflecting impairments in both rapid feedforward and slower feedback-based control mechanisms. In addition, impaired vocal compensatory behavior was associated with reduced functional connectivity between pSTG and the left dorsal precentral speech areas (dPSA) as well as the right dorsal laryngeal motor cortex (dLMC), suggesting the critical role of these networks in auditory-feedback-based laryngeal motor control during vocal production and their stroke-induced impairment in aphasia. Conclusions Our data provide converging evidence of disrupted auditory-motor integration and impaired neural communications within dorsal stream networks in aphasia. Significance These findings emphasize that clinical interventions for aphasia therapy benefit from targeting sensorimotor mechanisms supporting vocal auditory feedback processing and control. Personalized interventions that strengthen sensorimotor integration pathways could further enhance recovery of fluent verbal communication.

item.title: Aging Is Associated with Reduced Topographic Differentiation Between Speaking and Silent Reading
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Aging affects how neural activity is organized and specialized, but its impact on neural differentiation across language tasks remains unclear. In this study, we investigated whether aging influences neural differentiation during speaking and silent reading. Fifteen young adults and 15 older adults completed speaking and silent-reading tasks in a delayed-response paradigm while we collected electroencephalography (EEG) data. We examined EEG signal strength using time-resolved global field power (GFP), spatial configuration using topographic analysis of variance (TANOVA), and task-specific neural differentiation using the global dissimilarity index (DISS). We also examined the relationship between neural and behavioral measures, including digit-span scores and speech onset time. We found that speaking was associated with higher GFP than silent reading in the 388–800 ms interval, with no significant effects of group or group × task interaction, indicating similar EEG strength across groups. TANOVA revealed age-related differences in scalp topography in the 229–334 ms and 377–538 ms intervals, a task effect in the 618–723 ms interval, and a group × task interaction in the 562–636 ms interval. Notably, young adults had greater DISS than older adults during the 508–629 ms and 660–800 ms intervals, reflecting more distinct neural configurations for speaking and reading. We did not find significant correlations between DISS or GFP and behavioral measures, and the two groups performed similarly on behavioral measures. Overall, aging was associated with reduced neural differentiation between speaking and silent reading, especially during later processing stages (e.g., motor command preparation), while preserving overall EEG activity and behavioral performance. These findings may suggest that aging reduces neural network specificity (as previously suggested) and alters spatial organization without necessarily impairing behavior.

item.title: Sublexical compensatory reorganization of Chinese character recognition in Alzheimer's disease.
item.description:
Journal of clinical and experimental neuropsychology
Objective This study investigated the cognitive-functional shift in visual character recognition across the cognitive decline trajectory, ranging from healthy aging through Mild Cognitive Impairment (MCI) to Mild Alzheimer's Disease (AD). Specifically, it was hypothesized that as global semantic networks degrade, the reliance on rapid holistic processing decreases, prompting a compensatory shift toward sublexical features. Method Using a controlled unmasked priming lexical decision paradigm, this study evaluated behavioral performance across three distinct participant groups (N = 30 per group): healthy controls (HC), individuals with MCI, and patients with Mild AD. The experimental stimuli consisted of 80 Chinese phonograms matched across key psycholinguistic properties. This study utilized mixed-design Analyses of Variance (ANOVAs) alongside item-level hierarchical multiple regression (HMR) models to isolate the specific drivers of reaction times, assessing the predictive power of visual complexity, whole-character frequency, semantic transparency, and phonetic regularity. Results The analytical models revealed distinctly divergent psycholinguistic trajectories. The HC group demonstrated highly efficient holistic processing, with performance primarily driven by whole-character frequency. Conversely, the MCI group exhibited a unique transitional cognitive profile, characterized by a simultaneous reliance on both holistic whole-word access and analytic sublexical features. Crucially, in the Mild AD tgroup, the holistic processing advantage was entirely abolished. This functional disintegration triggered a compensatory reorganization toward bottom-up sublexical properties, with patients relying heavily on semantic transparency and phonetic regularity to achieve semantic access. Conclusions These findings demonstrate a linguistic Compensation-Related Utilization of Neural Circuits Hypothesis (CRUNCH) effect within the degenerating brain. As top-down lexical-semantic hubs deteriorate, reflected behaviorally in this paradigm by the loss of holistic processing advantages, the cognitive system actively compensates by upregulating bottom-up, sublexical pathways. Furthermore, the transitional sublexical dependency observed during the MCI stage highlights the translational potential of psycholinguistic variables as sensitive, noninvasive behavioral biomarkers for the early screening and monitoring of dementia.

item.title: Bridging language phenotypes, neural dynamics and gene regulation in autism.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Autism Spectrum Disorders (ASDs) affect approximately 1% of the global population, with prevalence rising over recent decades. Although ASDs are heritable (~70%), translating genetic findings into effective therapeutics remains challenging due to the vast number of implicated risk genes (>700) and the limited influence of individual genes on disease expression. Their collective impact and convergent expression patterns of small-effect genes provide insights into ASD-related neurobiological mechanisms. Current interventions remain symptom-focused and do not address underlying neurodevelopmental mechanisms. Emerging approaches in functional genomics offer new insights into ASD pathogenesis by exploring gene expression diversity, yet clinical applications remain distant. Language deficits are among the most frequent and disabling features of ASD, profoundly affecting individuals' and families' quality of life. Recent evidence from neuroimaging and electrophysiology studies suggests disrupted neural oscillatory dynamics are linked to language deficits in ASD. Several ASD-associated genes have been implicated in biological pathways involved in the regulation of brain oscillatory dynamics, suggesting a potential mechanistic link between genetic variation, altered brain rhythms, and language impairment. We propose a neurophysiological imaging genetics framework that leverages neural oscillatory profiles as endophenotypes for targeted investigation and as functional readouts of gene expression. Within this framework, neuromodulation is proposed as an experimental approach to investigate and potentially modulate altered oscillatory dynamics associated with speech communication deficits in ASD, while integrating oscillation-related ASD candidate genes into a symptom-oriented model of functional genomics. This approach shows how integrating genetic variation, non-invasive neuroimaging, and behavioral phenotypes can advance our understanding of ASD and inform targeted, mechanism-based interventions.

item.title: Multiscale neural signatures of long-lag repetition learning: a simultaneous fNIRS-EEG study.
item.description:
Neurophotonics
Significance Repetition-based learning supports word recognition and reading fluency, yet its neural mechanisms remain poorly understood, particularly where deficits in consolidating repeated linguistic input may underlie reading and language difficulties. Establishing reliable neural markers of repetition-based learning is a critical first step toward characterizing the phenotypes of these difficulties in children. Aim We developed a whole-brain simultaneous functional near-infrared spectroscopy-electroencephalography (fNIRS-EEG) approach to capture fast temporal electrophysiological and spatially accurate hemodynamic signals during long-lag repetition learning. Approach Thirty participants performed a semantic judgment task with words repeated across four runs with intervening items, modeling repetition demands central to reading instruction. A multimodal decoding framework integrating electrophysiological, hemodynamic, and cross-modal fNIRS-EEG correlation features was used to classify repetition-based learning. Results Repeated words showed response time reductions. EEG captured a frontal N400-range repetition-related negativity and attenuation of alpha-beta suppression, reflecting changes in recognition-related and post-recognition processing. fNIRS revealed left inferior frontal and superior temporal efficiency increases alongside right supramarginal activation, suggesting integrative processing. Multimodal classifiers outperformed unimodal classifiers, indicating that each modality captured complementary aspects of learning. Conclusions Combining fNIRS and EEG with multimodal machine learning provides a richer characterization of repetition-based learning than either modality alone, establishing a framework for phenotyping language learning capacity and identifying neural markers of reading difficulties in pediatric populations.

item.title: Involuntary facial muscle activity during imagined vocalisation contaminates EEG and enables emotion decoding.
item.description:
Journal of neural engineering
Objective. Decoding imagined speech from electroencephalography (EEG) recordings is potentially useful for brain-computer interfaces. Previous studies have focused on decoding semantic information from EEG, leaving the decoding of emotion - an important component of human communication - largely unexplored.Approach. Here, we report two experiments involving participants tasked with overt (n = 14) or imagined (n = 21) emotional vocalisation in five different categories: anger, happiness, neutral, sadness, and pleasure. Throughout, we recorded 64-channel EEG; we computed time-frequency features and used a logistic-regression classifier to evaluate emotion decoding accuracy. In five participants, we also recorded facial surface electromyography (sEMG) during imagined vocalisation, and studied the contamination of EEG by sEMG.Main results. Our results show that emotion can be decoded from single-trial EEG recordings of both overt (78.1%, chance = 20%) and imagined vocalisation (36.4%). The high-gamma band (50 to 100 Hz) and lateral EEG channels (T7, T8, and proximal) were important for decoding. sEMG analysis indicated that involuntary facial muscle activity contributed to these spectral and spatial patterns during imagined vocalisation. We identified a prominent muscle-induced pattern over lateral EEG channels - the railroad cross-tie pattern - showing greater activation during imagined happy vocalisations. We conclude that involuntary facial muscle activity is associated with certain emotion categories (i.e. happiness) and contributes to the decoding of emotion from single-trial EEG recordings.Significance. This study provides converging EEG and sEMG evidence demonstrating that involuntary facial muscle activity occurs during imagined vocalisation and is modulated by emotion, producing emotion-specific EEG contamination patterns. Although we focused on imagined vocalisations, the EMG patterns we observed closely resembled EEG patterns commonly reported in emotion decoding studies, raising concerns about involuntary facial muscle activity in such work.

item.title: Differentiating non-fluent and logopenic primary progressive aphasia via automated acoustic speech analysis.
item.description:
Cortex; a journal devoted to the study of the nervous system and behavior
In primary progressive aphasia, differential diagnosis between non-fluent (nfvPPA) and logopenic (lvPPA) variants can be clinically challenging. Although linguistic features from connected speech may aid in PPA subtype classification, they depend on labor-intensive transcriptions. In contrast, acoustic features are extracted directly from the audio signal and have shown potential in capturing variant-specific patterns, but their diagnostic relevance is not well understood. In this study, we analyzed connected speech recordings from 242 individuals (40 healthy controls, 91 lvPPA, 111 nfvPPA) performing a ∼2-min picture description task. We extracted 103 acoustic features from each recording and reduced them to 9, which we finally grouped into four domain scores representing speech rate and voice quality. Domain scores were tested as predictors in classification models to detect PPA and distinguish between PPA variants. Voxel-based morphometry was used to investigate brain-behavior relationships. Classification models combining the four domain scores and MMSE yielded 88% balanced-sample accuracy for PPA-versus-controls and 73% accuracy for lvPPA-versus-nfvPPA. Pitch and speech rate were the most discriminative markers. Voxel-based morphometry associated speech rate with the frontal speech production network, pitch with the middle frontal and inferior frontal gyrus, perturbation with the insula, and spectrum with the basal ganglia and the thalamus. We showed that acoustic analysis of brief speech samples has the potential to aid the diagnostic process and contribute to more nuanced phenotyping. With further validation, such measures could be integrated into clinical workflows as low-burden, objective tools to support differential diagnosis and track disease progression in PPA.

item.title: Speech Tracking in fMRI Reveals a Distinct Response to Sentence Boundaries During Comprehension
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Psycholinguistic research and linguistic theory suggest that comprehending continuous speech involves segmenting it into sentences. Yet, direct neuroimaging evidence for this process remains scarce, partly because sentence boundaries coincide with acoustic, prosodic, lexical, and syntactic changes. Here, we used whole-brain fMRI to test whether sentence boundaries elicit a neural response beyond these accompanying speech properties during spontaneous speech comprehension. We modelled BOLD responses to sentence-final words alongside continuous regressors characterizing accompanying speech properties. This approach revealed sensitivity to continuously varying features of speech across multiple brain regions. Notably, the acoustic envelope predicted BOLD responses in bilateral primary auditory cortices. Responses associated with prosodic breaks and emphasis were found in right temporal cortex, syntactic bottom-up node count in the left superior temporal sulcus, and word concreteness in the parahippocampal gyri. Critically, sentence-final words were associated with an increased activation in right temporal regions, after accounting for acoustic, prosodic, lexical, semantic and syntactic properties. These findings provide evidence for a neural response to sentence boundaries consistent with active sentence segmentation. More generally, this study demonstrates the value of continuous-regressor modelling for investigating speech comprehension with fMRI.

item.title: Time at Home for Whom? Unequal Returns of Paid Family Leave for Infant White Matter and Language Development
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Paid family leave (PFL) may give parents more time with infants, ease financial strain, and support stable routines. Although PFL has been linked to child development, little is known about neural pathways that might underpin its benefits or whether associations vary across families. Using data from 274 infants in the HEALthy Brain and Child Development Study, we examined associations of maternal and paternal PFL with language ability at 12 months and white matter microstructure at 6 months. We tested whether associations varied by the corresponding parent’s education. Neither maternal nor paternal PFL was directly associated with language scores or fractional anisotropy in the left arcuate, inferior longitudinal, or uncinate fasciculus. Maternal education moderated associations between maternal PFL and fractional anisotropy in the arcuate ( p = .014) and inferior longitudinal fasciculus ( p = .003; n = 148). In both tracts, PFL was associated with higher fractional anisotropy only among infants whose mothers had relatively high education. No comparable pattern emerged for language, the uncinate fasciculus, or paternal PFL. Findings suggest that the neurodevelopmental correlates of PFL may depend on family resources rather than operate uniformly across families, underscoring the need to pair paid leave with additional supports and resources. Lay Summary Paid family leave may give parents more time at home, steadier daily routines, and less financial worry in the months after a birth, all of which could change the care an infant receives. But these benefits may not be equal across families. In a national study of infants, we examined whether paid leave taken by mothers, fathers or partners was related to early language skills and to the organization of brain pathways involved in language. Paid leave was not directly related to language scores or brain development overall. However, maternal paid leave was associated with more mature organization in two language-related brain pathways only among infants whose mothers had higher levels of education. No similar pattern was found for father or partner leave. These findings suggest that paid leave alone may not reduce early developmental disparities, and that policies offering paid leave may need to be paired with additional support for families with fewer resources.

item.title: Evidence for hierarchical representations of written and spoken words from an open-science human neuroimaging dataset.
item.description:
Imaging neuroscience (Cambridge, Mass.)
Reading and speech recognition rely on multi-level processing that builds from basic visual or sound features to complete word representations, yet details of these processing hierarchies (in particular those for spoken words) are still poorly understood. We re-analyzed the functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data provided in the Mother Of all Unification Studies (MOUS) open-science dataset by using parametric regressions of word frequency and sublexical unit (bigram or syllable) frequency during reading and speech listening tasks in order to elucidate lexical and sublexical processing stages in the visual and auditory modalities. We first validated our approach in the written word domain, where the technique identified significant correlations for word frequency in the left mid-fusiform cortex (at the location of the Visual Word Form Area) and a left occipital region tracking bigram frequency, compatible with prior reports. During listening, activity in a left mid-superior temporal region consistent with the recently described Auditory Word Form Area (AWFA) showed a lexical frequency effect, while a more posterior region of the superior temporal gyrus was sensitive to syllable frequency. Activation in the left inferior frontal gyrus correlated with both written and spoken word frequencies. These findings suggest analogous posterior-to-anterior hierarchical organizations in the anteroventral visual and auditory streams, with modality-specific posterior sublexical and more anterior lexical representations that converge in higher-order language areas.

item.title: Longitudinal associations of screen time with brain development and expressive language skills in early childhood.
item.description:
iScience
Screen-based media may reduce reciprocal social interactions that support expressive language development, but little is known about how early language abilities, later screen use, and brain structure are related during toddlerhood. We examined 70 toddlers with structural magnetic resonance imaging and standardized developmental assessments at age 2, along with parent-reported screen time at ages 2 and 3. Greater weekday and weekend screen time at age 2 were associated with poorer concurrent expressive language skills. Right pars triangularis volume did not explain additional variance in these cross-sectional associations. Longitudinally, right pars triangularis volume moderated the association between expressive language skills at age 2 and screen time at age 3. Among toddlers with relatively smaller right pars triangularis volumes, poorer expressive language skills were associated with greater subsequent weekday and weekend screen time. These findings support guidance to limit screen use during toddlerhood, a sensitive window for language and brain development.

item.title: Impact of sedation on the reliability of magnetoencephalographic language mapping in pediatric epilepsy.
item.description:
Epilepsia
Objective Magnetoencephalography (MEG) language mapping in pediatric epilepsy frequently requires sedation, which may alter cortical physiology and compromise the reliability of language lateralization. We hypothesized that sedation disrupts coupling between early auditory processing and higher order language networks, reducing the interpretability of laterality metrics. Methods Sixty-nine pediatric patients undergoing presurgical MEG evaluation were analyzed, including 32 nonsedated and 37 sedated participants. Auditory evoked field responses were quantified using the M200/M100 amplitude ratio and interhemispheric asymmetry. Language laterality indices (LIs) were derived from a continuous recognition memory paradigm, and source localization was performed using Fast-VESTAL. Results Sedation preferentially suppressed late auditory responses, reflected by a significant reduction in the M200/M100 ratio (p < .001) and increased interindividual variability. Despite preserved early sensory responses, auditory-language coupling was numerically attenuated under sedation. Notably, low M200/M100 ratios were frequently associated with highly lateralized LI values, suggesting reduced physiological reliability and the potential for "false certainty" in language lateralization. Source imaging demonstrated preserved primary auditory cortical activity with reduced recruitment of higher order association networks in sedated participants. Significance Sedation compromises the physiological reliability of MEG language lateralization by disrupting late auditory and association-level processing. The M200/M100 ratio provides a practical physiological marker for identifying cases in which laterality results should be interpreted with caution. These findings support a physiology-informed framework for improving the clinical interpretation of MEG language mapping in sedated pediatric patients, with direct implications for presurgical planning in pediatric epilepsy.

item.title: Language-associated brain representations covary with disruption of selfhood under psilocybin
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Language helps organise experience into an idiosyncratic, temporally extended sense of self. We therefore used fMRI to investigate whether greater similarity between subjects in the activity of language-associated brain regions accompanied psilocybin-induced loss of selfhood using fMRI. Participants heard music and viewed moving clouds at baseline and after 19 mg psilocybin. At each brain location and time point, we tested whether similarity increased with each pair’s summed rank on the Ego Dissolution Inventory (EDI; N=43). We grouped independent components of these associations by time course and decoded each group’s map with Neurosynth. Elementary visual imagery (SI; N=49) and baseline activity served as comparators. Under psilocybin, one group formed a distributed, left-lateralised frontotemporal network matching the Neurosynth language map (r=.382, spatial-null p<.001, q=.003), nearly twice the largest comparator estimate (SI: r=.208, p=.004, q=.028; baseline: r≤.12). In exploratory analyses, resting-state connectivity of this network decreased with posterior visual cortex and increased with thalamic and frontal regions. Participants with higher EDI scores showed larger changes (ρ=.455, Bonferroni-adjusted p=.048; SI: ρ=.008), most strongly for items describing loss of ego or identity (ρ=.43–.51; other items, ρ=.22–.33). We propose that language-associated systems incorporate each person’s semantic and autobiographical context into experience, and that disrupting them contributes to loss of ego and identity.

item.title: White matter differences in adults with developmental language disorder
item.description:
[预印本] PsyArXiv
Developmental language disorder is a highly common yet underdiagnosed neurodevelopmental disorder which impacts receptive and/or expressive language abilities and cannot be attributed to another etiology such as hearing loss or a lack of early exposure to language. There is very little research into the brain differences that characterize developmental language disorder, especially in adult populations In this study, we used diffusion MRI to determine whether adults with DLD show differences in white matter microstructure of the brain when compared to adults with typical language. Participants included 23 adults identified as meeting criteria for developmental language disorder, as well as a group of 26 adults with typical language. White matter microstructure was examined with fractional anisotropy via diffusion tensor imaging and precise biophysical models of intra-axonal signal fraction and orientation coherence via the Standard Model of diffusion imaging, using tractometry to evaluate microstructure differences along white matter tracts. Analysis showed reduced myelin integrity in DLD in the corpus callosum, but increased myelin integrity in the left superior longitudinal fasciculus.
