It is yet unclear whether differences exist in childhood and are retained into adulthood, are a result of different language environments during childhood, or are a result of behavioral and neural compensation.

item.title: Rapid parameter-efficient calibration for cross-session intracortical speech decoding across multiple datasets
item.description:
[预印本] Research Square
Abstract Intracortical speech brain–computer interfaces (BCIs) can restore communication for people who cannot speak, but longitudinal neural variability can degrade decoding across sessions. We implemented a parameter-efficient cross-session calibration framework using separate recurrent connectionist temporal classification (CTC) decoders for two public intracortical speech datasets (T12 and T15). Adaptation was restricted to a 256 × 256 affine transformation and bias at the neural input, while the recurrent encoder and CTC classifier remained frozen. Sessions were split chronologically; the calibration protocol was selected only on T12 validation sessions, frozen before later T12 testing, and transferred unchanged to T15. Only 65,792 parameters (<0.05% of either model) were updated using 40 or 80 labeled trials. On T12, macro phoneme error rate improved by 11.37% and 15.51%, with all six held-out sessions improving under all three seeds. On T15, improvements were 2.72% and 10.05%, revealing greater session dependence. Extending prior work on high-performance and rapidly calibrating speech neuroprostheses, this study tests a fixed lightweight calibration rule across two independent datasets under a validation-locked protocol. These findings provide a leakage-resistant cross-dataset evaluation of rapid longitudinal recalibration and show that input-space adaptation can recover a substantial, but not universal, component of cross-session mismatch.

item.title: Passive Language Mapping With High-Gamma Modulations.
item.description:
Journal of clinical neurophysiology : official publication of the American Electroencephalographic Society
Summary Passive language mapping using high-gamma modulation (HGM) has emerged as a valuable tool in both presurgical evaluation for epilepsy and neuroscientific discovery. HGM mapping leverages task-related synchronization in high-gamma frequencies to identify language areas without the risks associated with electrical stimulation mapping. This review outlines the principles and techniques used in the field of HGM-based mapping, including electrode types, referencing schemes, power analysis, and localization techniques. We survey a range of cognitive tasks-speech production, auditory processing, reading, and memory-that elicit language-related HGM responses and discuss their relevance to comprehensive language mapping. We examine perspectives on methodologic challenges, including artifact management, variability across patients, and spatial sampling. We assess validation studies comparing HGM with electrical stimulation mapping and neuropsychological outcomes, noting HGM's unique role in identifying language cortex in pediatric and cognitively impaired populations. Finally, we speculate on the future directions of the field, including integration with corticocortical evoked potentials and the potential for HGM-informed speech synthesis. As the field matures, HGM mapping is poised to contribute to improved clinical outcomes and enhance our understanding of the dynamics and development of the human language network.

item.title: Technological interventions in dyslexia: a neurobiological perspective of language learning.
item.description:
Disability and rehabilitation. Assistive technology
Objective Developmental dyslexia is a neurodevelopmental language learning disorder characterised by persistent difficulty in phonological processing and fluent word recognition. To address these challenges, a range of interventions has been developed to support reading acquisition and fluency. These interventions include a promising field of technological aids that cater to a broader audience. However, the limited understanding of the neurobiological effects of technological interventions restricts significant evaluation of their effectiveness. The paper examines the influence of technological interventions on the neural mechanisms that support reading in individuals with developmental dyslexia. Methods This narrative review maintains methodological precision by focusing exclusively on literature that bridges the gap between instructional technology and its neurobiological outcomes, offering an integrated analysis of behavioural and neurobiological shifts in literacy development. Impact The findings suggest that the technological interventions enhance phonological processing efficiency by strengthening neurocognitive networks and promoting compensatory activation patterns. However, these results cannot be widely generalised due to the inconsistencies in intervention design and methodological rigour. Thus, to take a closer look at the efficacy of technological interventions, this paper aims to offer a comprehensive neurobiological review of the effects of interventions and assistive technologies, highlighting the neural and behavioural outcomes while pointing to unresolved questions for future investigation.

item.title: Semantic working memory supports phrasal planning: Evidence from acute stroke.
item.description:
Neuropsychologia
This study examined the contribution of semantic and phonological working memory (WM) to lexical-semantic planning during language production for individuals tested acutely after left-hemisphere stroke. Participants completed tasks assessing phrase and sentence production, single-word retrieval, semantic and phonological WM, and single-word input processing. Using a constrained production paradigm that manipulated structure (phrase vs. sentence) and number of adjectival modifiers (one vs. two), we found that semantic WM capacity, indexed by performance on a category probe task, predicted accuracy in producing phrases containing multiple content words, even after controlling for single-word processing abilities. In contrast, phonological WM capacity, indexed by performance on a digit matching span task, did not relate to production accuracy. The relation to semantic WM was specific to the condition with the largest number of content words within a phrase (two-adjective noun phrase). These findings support the contention that lexical-semantic planning occurs phrase by phrase and is constrained by the capacity of a semantic maintenance buffer that supports activation and maintenance of multiple lexical-semantic representations prior to articulation. In contrast, phonological planning appears to operate within a narrower window that makes few demands on phonological WM. The results converge with prior neuropsychological evidence linking semantic WM to phrase-level planning and further imply that the phrase serves as the default scope of lexical-semantic encoding in production. Implications for models of WM and language production are discussed.

item.title: The role of world knowledge in sentence comprehension under working-memory constraints: An fMRI study
item.description:
[预印本] bioRxiv
Introduction Comprehension of thematic roles, i.e., “who did what to whom,” relies on limited cognitive resources, and constraints on these resources can alter the use of plausibility information derived from world knowledge. Although sentence-processing studies have described how plausibility information constrains interpretation, it remains unclear how this process is supported by the architecture of working memory. This study examines whether the phonological loop, one of the components of working memory, contributes to thematic-role processing based on world knowledge. Methods Using articulatory suppression and functional magnetic resonance imaging, we examined whether constraining the function of the phonological loop modulates behavioral and neural responses to sentences in which syntactically assigned thematic roles are plausible or implausible given world knowledge. To constrain the phonological loop, we manipulated the task: a single task and a dual task involving concurrent articulation. Results We found no significant interaction between task and plausibility, although equivalence analyses did not provide evidence for the absence of a plausibility effect during articulation. In contrast, a robust main effect of thematic-role plausibility was observed: implausible sentences elicited greater activation than plausible sentences in the left inferior frontal gyrus (LIFG) and medial superior frontal gyrus (mSFG) at the whole-brain level, and in both the pars triangularis and pars orbitalis of the LIFG in the ROI analyses. Discussion These findings provide no conclusive evidence that constraining the phonological loop substantially modulates the use of world knowledge in comprehension of thematic roles, while also leaving open the possibility of a smaller task-dependent effect. At the same time, the robust neural responses to implausibility indicate that the LIFG and mSFG consistently contribute to the processing of plausibility information derived from world knowledge.

item.title: Openness to experience modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing.
item.description:
Physiology & behavior
Personality fundamentally shapes language processing, yet the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying this relationship remain poorly understood. Openness to experience (Openness), as measured by the NEO Five-Factor Inventory (NEO-FFI), has been associated with enhanced creativity and engagement with novel semantic information. This study examined how openness modulates the neural dynamics of semantic processing using event-related potentials (ERPs) during a semantic category verification task. Participants evaluated category relatedness across the four levels of semantic structure, including high typicality (HT), low typicality (LT), related violations (RV), and nonrelated violations (NRV). Neural responses exhibited the expected graded pattern, with N400 amplitudes becoming more negative as semantic relatedness decreased. Critically, higher Openness was associated with greater N400 differentiation between related and nonrelated violations, an effect uniquely predicted by Openness beyond the remaining four personality traits. Follow-up analyses revealed that this differentiation was primarily driven by enhanced N400 responses to nonrelated violations rather than by reduced responses to related violations. This pattern is inconsistent with a simple facilitation account in which higher Openness uniformly eases semantic processing. Instead, it suggests that Openness is associated with heightened sensitivity to semantic mismatch or more sustained semantic evaluation when incoming information is incompatible with an activated context. Behavioral performance was comparable across participants; the observed neural differences were not accompanied by detectable differences in task success. Together, these findings establish that Openness is systematically related to variation in the neural dynamics of semantic processing, while highlighting the need to clarify the underlying cognitive mechanisms and contributions of other individual differences.

item.title: Neurophysiological signatures underlying preserved lexical-semantic proficiency in healthy aging.
item.description:
Neurobiology of aging
Although semantic cognition remains behaviorally stable with age, neuroimaging studies report age-related alterations in response to semantic context. To address these inconsistent findings, we combined behavioral and magnetoencephalography (MEG) measures and examined the neural mechanisms underlying lexical-semantic processing in healthy aging. Forty-six Finnish-speaking adults across younger (22 - 32 years) and older (62 - 69 years) cohorts performed a semantic congruency judgment task on word pairs. Both age groups performed the task with high accuracy, with older adults responding faster than younger. While task performance was retained in older adults, MEG revealed a shift in the neural activation patterns with advancing age. Younger participants exhibited the canonical N400 effect in the left temporal cortex 300 - 400 ms post-stimulus, followed by a late semantic effect, whereas older adults showed less pronounced congruency effects, and the activation distribution was shifted toward frontal and bilateral regions. Despite the absence of the canonical N400 effect in older participants, multivariate time-resolved decoding demonstrated that the congruency effect was decodable from the MEG activation patterns in both groups from ~300 ms post-stimulus, indicating preserved sensitivity to congruency with age. Decoding performance further correlated with response times, suggesting that greater neural separation between semantic concepts, indicated by higher decodability, is associated with rapid decision-making. Critically, age groups were distinguishable based on their neural responses 300 - 800 ms post-stimulus, indicating a functional reorganization of semantic processing in older adults. Overall, our findings suggest that healthy aging involves a reconfiguration of neural systems associated with preserved semantic proficiency, despite broader age-related cognitive changes.

item.title: Altered frontal and dorsal hemodynamic engagement during mandarin aspiration processing in post-stroke aphasia: an fNIRS study.
item.description:
Brain and language
Auditory and speech-perception difficulties are common in post-stroke aphasia (PSA), but cortical responses during passive listening to Mandarin speech remain underexplored. Seventeen Mandarin-speaking individuals with PSA and 18 matched healthy controls listened to auditory oddball blocks containing /ba/ standards and /pa/ deviants during functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS). Although these syllables instantiate an aspiration contrast strongly cued by voice onset time (VOT), standard and deviant trials were combined within a single block-level condition. The resulting measures therefore indexed activation during speech-containing blocks relative to silent inter-block intervals rather than phonemic discrimination, categorization, or VOT-specific processing. Seven theory-driven channels covering bilateral auditory, sensorimotor, inferior frontal, and dorsolateral prefrontal regions were analyzed using three HbO indices: β coefficient, peak amplitude, and temporal centroid. The PSA group showed an overall reduction in task-related HbO activation, reflected by a significant Group effect for the β coefficient. Peak amplitude also showed significant Group and Group × Channel effects, although no individual channel remained significant after correction for multiple comparisons. Temporal centroid showed no significant group or interaction effects. These findings provide preliminary evidence for reduced block-evoked cortical recruitment during passive auditory exposure to Mandarin speech sounds in PSA. Because the analysis did not include a direct standard-deviant or active auditory control comparison, the findings do not establish a selective impairment of phonemic discrimination, categorization, or VOT processing. Because patients were assessed 6-7 months after stroke onset, the activation differences may reflect both persistent impairment and recovery-related reorganization during the early chronic stage.
